amendments.rule: A repeated or resumptive element that the ASV renders once is still its own unit. Mark the unrepresented occurrence `unrepresented` rather than folding it into the rendered one. Where the repetition is a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral — Hebrew writes one `שָׁנָה` per numeral group where the ASV writes a single *years* — the rendered occurrence is the last, closing the whole Hebrew figure as the English noun closes the whole English one. Do not settle it by number agreement: Hebrew writes `שָׁנִים` after 2–10 and `שָׁנָה` from 11 up whatever the total, while the English plural follows the sum, so a match between them is an accident of two unrelated agreement systems and is not evidence. Do not settle it by which numeral the English noun stands beside either, since English drives the counted noun to the end of the phrase whatever order the translation chose. Tail-to-tail is what survives, and it holds across both Hebrew group orders and the ASV's frequent reordering of them. The genealogies are where this recurs, and BSB, which attaches the noun to its own phrase, disagrees on every first occurrence. **Tail-to-tail governs a run of absolute occurrences only.** Where the phrase is instead headed by a **construct** — a regnal date such as `בִּשְׁנַת עֶשְׂרִים וָשֶׁבַע שָׁנָה` → *In the twenty and seventh year* — the construct is what the English realizes, and the trailing absolute is the resumptive occurrence that goes `unrepresented`. So the rendered occurrence is the last of several absolutes but the first where a construct heads them, and MACULA's morphology is what decides which case this is. Position is the consequence, not the rule. **But a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused English word is not an unrendered occurrence.** Where a relative clause resumes its antecedent with a pronominal suffix on a preposition, or with a resumptive adverb, and the ASV writes one pronominal adverb for the whole — *wherein*, *whereon*, *whereby*, *whither*, and the bare *therein* of a preposition and its own suffix — the relative, the preposition and the resumptive morpheme share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, or on the preposition where no relative stands. Do not mark the suffix `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence: rule 30's one-English-word condition is met, because that word carries the resumption as well as the relation, exactly as *Nor* carries both the coordination and the negation in rule 35. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` → *wherein* as one three-morpheme unit in twenty-one places and `בָּהּ` → *therein* as one two-morpheme unit in sixty-one, and records no unit where such a suffix stands outside the word. So ask first whether the English word carries the morpheme's sense: what this rule's first sentence governs is an element the ASV has left unwritten, as a second `בֵּין` or a surplus `שָׁנָה` is, and not one it has written inside a fusion. **But read whether the ASV has written one English word or two before reading a fusion there.** Where it renders the relative and the preposition by two separate English words — *upon which*, *in which*, *with whom* — rule 30's one-English-word condition is unmet, rule 2 splits them, and each of the two morphemes takes the word written for it, the relative taking the relative pronoun and the preposition taking its own. The resumptive suffix is then the occurrence the ASV has left unwritten and is its own `unrepresented` unit under this rule's first sentence, since the relative pronoun already carries the resumption; this is the division rule 43 makes in `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ מוּם` → *that hath a blemish*, where two morphemes point at the antecedent and the ASV writes one word for it. Do not instead give the relative pronoun to the suffix under rule 18 and mark the written relative `unrepresented`: what that rule places is a relative in a clause with no relative morpheme in it, and a present morpheme takes its English before another reading does, as rules 46 and 47 direct. One chapter may write both shapes for one and the same Hebrew clause, and JDG.16.26 → *the pillars* ***whereupon*** *the house resteth* and JDG.16.29 → *the two middle pillars* ***upon which*** *the house rested* do. **The interrogative `אֵי` with a following `זֶה` is one interrogative expression, and its demonstrative is not an unrendered occurrence either.** Where the ASV renders `אֵי־זֶה` by a single interrogative word — *where*, *what*, *which* — the two morphemes share one unit under rule 30, headed on `אֵי`, which carries the wh-lexeme; the demonstrative is enclitic to the compound rather than a repeated or resumptive element, so this rule's first sentence does not reach it and it is never marked `unrepresented` beside a rendered `אֵי`. A construction-supplied copula joining that unit does not defeat rule 30's one-rendering condition, exactly as it does not for `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*, so `אֵי־זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ` → ***Where is*** *the way* fuses as `אֵי־זֶה` → *what* does. The corpus fuses this compound in every unit it records — JER.6.16, 1KI.13.12, ISA.66.1 twice, ECC.11.6 and 1KI.22.24 — and splits it in none. Two limits. Where the ASV spends a word on each morpheme, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits them as usual. And this governs `אֵי־זֶה` and no other pair: a deictic `זֶה` standing after an interrogative that keeps its own English word — the `זֶה` of `לָמָּה זֶּה` or of `בֶּן־מִי־זֶה`, and the `זֶה` of `מִי זֶה` where the ASV writes *this* for it — is this rule's ordinary case, rendered where the ASV writes a word for it and `unrepresented` where it does not. **A resumptive possessive suffix is read on exactly those terms, and it need not stand on a preposition.** Where the clause resumes its antecedent with a suffix on a noun inside it and the ASV writes one *whose* for the pair, the relative and that suffix share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, while the noun keeps its own English: `אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` → *a land* ***whose*** *stones are iron* is one unit on `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix, with *stones* left to `אֶבֶן`. Contiguity is not the condition, for the reason rule 35 gives: however much of the clause stands between them, the one English word still carries both the relation and the resumption, so nothing is left over to mark. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix as one *whose* unit at DEU.28.49 and 1KI.8.39, and as a `noncompositional` one at AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1 among eighteen such places. **But read which morphemes stand in each clause before counting a second occurrence.** Where a further clause is coordinated under the one written relative and the ASV rewrites its *whose* at the head of that clause, a resumptive suffix standing in that clause is what the second word realizes, under rule 18's sentence giving a suffix the English relative pronoun that renders it: `וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת` → *and out of* ***whose*** *hills thou mayest dig copper* gives its *whose* to the suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ`, not to the relative as a repetition under rule 25. Where no such suffix stands in the coordinated clause, rule 55's distributed subordinator governs as before and every occurrence is the relative's. **And read whether the suffix points at the antecedent at all before treating it as resumptive.** Every fusion above rests on a morpheme that resumes the antecedent, and a pronominal suffix standing inside the relative clause does that only where its referent is the antecedent; agreement is the first check and reference decides, so read MACULA's person, gender and number against the noun the clause modifies. Where the suffix instead denotes something else the clause speaks of, the one English pronominal adverb carries the relative's own relation and nothing of that suffix, rule 30's condition is unmet for it, and the fusion does not reach it: the relative takes the adverb alone, the suffix takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and the preposition it stands on is disposed of by rules 11 and 40 like any other. `וְאֶת־תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר־חִלָּה יְהוָה בָּהּ` → *and the sicknesses* ***wherewith*** *Jehovah hath made* ***it*** *sick* gives *wherewith* to `אֲשֶׁר` alone, *it* to the suffix of `בָּהּ`, which is feminine singular and denotes the land rather than the masculine plural `תַּחֲלֻאִים` the relative modifies, and leaves the `בְּ` `unrepresented` under rule 40, since the ASV promotes its object to the direct object of *made ... sick*. A relative left holding such a word by itself is not a unit short of its parts: the corpus aligns a bare `אֲשֶׁר` to *wherewith* in fifty-five units, and its *wherein* units include bare relatives beside the three-morpheme fusions. Count the English pronouns against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s: where the ASV writes a pronoun besides the adverb, some morpheme other than the relative answers for it, and where it writes none, the resumption is inside the adverb and the paragraphs above govern. **A distributive repetition is read on those same terms, and there the rendered occurrence is the first.** Where Hebrew joins a noun to a repetition of itself with a waw and the ASV writes one English noun with a distributive determiner standing before it — `לְשַׁעַר וָשָׁעַר` → *at* ***every gate***, and likewise *each* or *every one* — the first occurrence takes the noun's own English word together with that supplied determiner under rule 15, the waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 for want of a written connective, and the repeated occurrence is `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence. Do not fuse the three morphemes into one unit under rule 30: that rule's condition is one rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and the English noun is a word the ASV spends on this noun in particular, which the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use finds gone with it while the repetition and the coordination are left saying nothing either way. Tail-to-tail above governs a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral and does not reach this: what the ASV writes here is a determiner and a noun opening one phrase, and the first occurrence is where they stand, exactly as rule 47 reads a phrase's single *the* onto the first of the articles it opens. **But that reading rests on the single preposition opening the phrase, and a repetition whose occurrences each carry their own rendered preposition is not it.** Where Hebrew writes a preposition on each occurrence — `כְּפַעַם בְּפַעַם` → *as at other times* — and the ASV renders both prepositions and writes one English noun after the second, that noun stands inside the second phrase and the second occurrence is the rendered one, the first going `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence; read which preposition the English noun stands after, as rule 47 reads which word the phrase's single *the* stands before. Three limits. Where a single English word carries the whole repetition, spending nothing on either occurrence in particular — a lone adverb such as *daily* — rule 30's condition is met and the morphemes share one unit as before. Where the ASV writes a connective for the waw, or an English word for each occurrence, nothing is left unrendered, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. And where an article or another determiner morpheme stands on the noun, that morpheme takes the written determiner under rules 41 and 15 as it always does, since what this paragraph places is the repetition and not the determiner.
amendments.why: Two additions, both cases this chapter met that the rule as written does not decide. First: 16.26 and 16.29 write one and the same Hebrew clause — relative, preposition and resumptive suffix — as whereupon and as upon which. The fusion paragraph settles the one-word shape and the aei-zeh paragraph says in passing that a word spent on each morpheme defeats the condition, but nothing says which of the three morphemes is then left unrendered, and rule 18's sentence giving a suffix an English relative pronoun invites the opposite division: which to the suffix, the written relative unrepresented. The new paragraph settles it the way rule 43 already settles the same count for 'that hath a blemish', so no corpus row is contradicted. Second: the distributive paragraph directs the rendered occurrence to the first, reasoning from a determiner and noun opening one phrase after a single preposition; 16.20's doubled temporal noun carries a rendered preposition on each occurrence and the ASV's noun stands after the second, so the first-occurrence direction would put the noun in a phrase it does not stand in. The added sentence limits that paragraph to the shape it was written for and reads the other by the same which-word-does-it-stand-after test rule 47 uses. Nothing else in rule 22 is changed.

conventions: A relative with a preposition and a resumptive suffix pointing at its antecedent is fused or split by the number of English words the ASV writes, not by the Hebrew: 16.26 reads the three morphemes as one unit on whereupon under rules 22 and 30, and 16.29, whose Hebrew clause is the same, is split because the ASV writes upon which there - the relative takes which, the preposition takes upon, and the suffix is the unrendered resumption, unrepresented under rule 22. Do not read the pair as a chapter inconsistency, and do not give which to the suffix under rule 18 while marking the written relative unrepresented. 16.11 (wherewith) follows 16.26.

In the refrain 'wherein thy great strength lieth' (16.5, 16.6, 16.15) the ASV's lieth is the construction's linking verb for a verbless clause with an adjectival predicate, so it joins the adjective's unit and that unit heads on great (rule 20). It is not a supplied lexical verb: dropping it removes the link English writes for a predication the Hebrew has already made with the adjective, not the predication itself.

The noun rendered inner chamber (16.9, 16.12) heads on chamber, not on inner. The ASV writes chamber alone for this word, so inner is its specifier and rule 31's class-noun test keeps the head on the noun; the competing head on inner is named in both verse notes and was declined for the chapter as a whole.

In the doubled temporal phrase at 16.20 (rendered 'as at other times') the English noun goes to the second occurrence and the first is unrepresented, because each occurrence carries its own preposition and both prepositions are rendered, so the noun stands inside the second phrase. Rule 22's distributive paragraph, which gives the noun to the first occurrence, governs a repetition joined by a waw with a single preposition opening the phrase, and does not reach this shape.

The corpus fuses this compound in every unit it records — JER.6.16, 1KI.13.12, ISA.66.1 twice, ECC.11.6 and 1KI.22.24 — and splits it in none. Two limits. Where the ASV spends a word on each morpheme, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits them as usual. And this governs `אֵי־זֶה` and no other pair: a deictic `זֶה` standing after an interrogative that keeps its own English word — the `זֶה` of `לָמָּה זֶּה` or of `בֶּן־מִי־זֶה`, and the `זֶה` of `מִי זֶה` where the ASV writes *this* for it — is this rule's ordinary case, rendered where the ASV writes a word for it and `unrepresented` where it does not. **A resumptive possessive suffix is read on exactly those terms, and it need not stand on a preposition.** Where the clause resumes its antecedent with a suffix on a noun inside it and the ASV writes one *whose* for the pair, the relative and that suffix share one unit under rule 30, headed on the relative, while the noun keeps its own English: `אֶרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אֲבָנֶיהָ בַרְזֶל` → *a land* ***whose*** *stones are iron* is one unit on `אֲשֶׁר` and the suffix, with *stones* left to `אֶבֶן`. Contiguity is not the condition, for the reason rule 35 gives: however much of the clause stands between them, the one English word still carries both the relation and the resumption, so nothing is left over to mark. The corpus reads `אֲשֶׁר` with its resumptive suffix as one *whose* unit at DEU.28.49 and 1KI.8.39, and as a `noncompositional` one at AMO.2.9 and DAN.10.1 among eighteen such places. **But read which morphemes stand in each clause before counting a second occurrence.** Where a further clause is coordinated under the one written relative and the ASV rewrites its *whose* at the head of that clause, a resumptive suffix standing in that clause is what the second word realizes, under rule 18's sentence giving a suffix the English relative pronoun that renders it: `וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ תַּחְצֹב נְחֹשֶׁת` → *and out of* ***whose*** *hills thou mayest dig copper* gives its *whose* to the suffix on `הֲרָרֶיהָ`, not to the relative as a repetition under rule 25. Where no such suffix stands in the coordinated clause, rule 55's distributed subordinator governs as before and every occurrence is the relative's. **And read whether the suffix points at the antecedent at all before treating it as resumptive.** Every fusion above rests on a morpheme that resumes the antecedent, and a pronominal suffix standing inside the relative clause does that only where its referent is the antecedent; agreement is the first check and reference decides, so read MACULA's person, gender and number against the noun the clause modifies. Where the suffix instead denotes something else the clause speaks of, the one English pronominal adverb carries the relative's own relation and nothing of that suffix, rule 30's condition is unmet for it, and the fusion does not reach it: the relative takes the adverb alone, the suffix takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, and the preposition it stands on is disposed of by rules 11 and 40 like any other. `וְאֶת־תַּחֲלֻאֶיהָ אֲשֶׁר־חִלָּה יְהוָה בָּהּ` → *and the sicknesses* ***wherewith*** *Jehovah hath made* ***it*** *sick* gives *wherewith* to `אֲשֶׁר` alone, *it* to the suffix of `בָּהּ`, which is feminine singular and denotes the land rather than the masculine plural `תַּחֲלֻאִים` the relative modifies, and leaves the `בְּ` `unrepresented` under rule 40, since the ASV promotes its object to the direct object of *made ... sick*. A relative left holding such a word by itself is not a unit short of its parts: the corpus aligns a bare `אֲשֶׁר` to *wherewith* in fifty-five units, and its *wherein* units include bare relatives beside the three-morpheme fusions. Count the English pronouns against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s: where the ASV writes a pronoun besides the adverb, some morpheme other than the relative answers for it, and where it writes none, the resumption is inside the adverb and the paragraphs above govern. **A distributive repetition is read on those same terms, and there the rendered occurrence is the first.** Where Hebrew joins a noun to a repetition of itself with a waw and the ASV writes one English noun with a distributive determiner standing before it — `לְשַׁעַר וָשָׁעַר` → *at* ***every gate***, and likewise *each* or *every one* — the first occurrence takes the noun's own English word together with that supplied determiner under rule 15, the waw is `unrepresented` under rule 14 for want of a written connective, and the repeated occurrence is `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence. Do not fuse the three morphemes into one unit under rule 30: that rule's condition is one rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and the English noun is a word the ASV spends on this noun in particular, which the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use finds gone with it while the repetition and the coordination are left saying nothing either way. Tail-to-tail above governs a counted noun distributed across a compound numeral and does not reach this: what the ASV writes here is a determiner and a noun opening one phrase, and the first occurrence is where they stand, exactly as rule 47 reads a phrase's single *the* onto the first of the articles it opens. **But that reading rests on the single preposition opening the phrase, and a repetition whose occurrences each carry their own rendered preposition is not it.** Where Hebrew writes a preposition on each occurrence — `כְּפַעַם בְּפַעַם` → *as at other times* — and the ASV renders both prepositions and writes one English noun after the second, that noun stands inside the second phrase and the second occurrence is the rendered one, the first going `unrepresented` under this rule's first sentence; read which preposition the English noun stands after, as rule 47 reads which word the phrase's single *the* stands before. Three limits. Where a single English word carries the whole repetition, spending nothing on either occurrence in particular — a lone adverb such as *daily* — rule 30's condition is met and the morphemes share one unit as before. Where the ASV writes a connective for the waw, or an English word for each occurrence, nothing is left unrendered, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. And where an article or another determiner morpheme stands on the noun, that morpheme takes the written determiner under rules 41 and 15 as it always does, since what this paragraph places is the repetition and not the determiner.
amended.why: Two additions, both cases this chapter met that the rule as written does not decide. First: 16.26 and 16.29 write one and the same Hebrew clause — relative, preposition and resumptive suffix — as whereupon and as upon which. The fusion paragraph settles the one-word shape and the aei-zeh paragraph says in passing that a word spent on each morpheme defeats the condition, but nothing says which of the three morphemes is then left unrendered, and rule 18's sentence giving a suffix an English relative pronoun invites the opposite division: which to the suffix, the written relative unrepresented. The new paragraph settles it the way rule 43 already settles the same count for 'that hath a blemish', so no corpus row is contradicted. Second: the distributive paragraph directs the rendered occurrence to the first, reasoning from a determiner and noun opening one phrase after a single preposition; 16.20's doubled temporal noun carries a rendered preposition on each occurrence and the ASV's noun stands after the second, so the first-occurrence direction would put the noun in a phrase it does not stand in. The added sentence limits that paragraph to the shape it was written for and reads the other by the same which-word-does-it-stand-after test rule 47 uses. Nothing else in rule 22 is changed.

report: Cross-verse check found no split. Recurring constructions are analysed identically wherever source and ASV agree: the interrogative preposition phrase is fused as wherein/wherewith at 16.5, 6, 10, 13, 15 and split only at 16.5b where the ASV writes two words (by what means); the refrain 'The Philistines are upon thee, Samson' at 16.9, 12, 14, 20 gives the supplied The to the noun, the copula to the preposition and the bare vocative to the name; the prison-house chain fronts the rectum's article at 16.21 and 16.25 alike; the wayehi frame gives its that to the apodosis waw at 16.4, 16 and 25, while the two apodoses with no frame (16.18, 16.24) leave that waw unrepresented on the same count.

The one pair that looks like a split is not one. 16.26 (relative + preposition + resumptive suffix) fuses all three morphemes into whereupon; the identical Hebrew clause at 16.29 is split because the ASV writes upon which, the relative taking which, the preposition taking upon, and the resumptive suffix left unrepresented. Rule 30's one-English-word condition is what differs, and it differs because the ASV wrote one word in one verse and two in the other. Recorded as a convention and promoted as an amendment to rule 22, which so far settles only the fused case and does not say which of the three morphemes goes unrendered when two words are written.

Differences that are the ASV's and not the chapter's, checked and left as they stand: the participle's article rendered at 16.12 and unrendered at 16.9; the possessive lamed carrying had at 16.9 where 16.12's parallel clause writes only a copula; echad rendered another at 16.7 and 16.11 beside kol rendered any at 16.17; the object marker taking of at 16.29, where a marker stands, against the of and on carried by the verb at 16.3 and 16.21, where none does.

The eleven added units are internally consistent. Supplied object pronouns are added wherever no object morpheme stands (16.2, 3, 14, 31) and go to the suffix or marker wherever one does (16.21). The supplied And and the supplied it was told at 16.2 are two units because they do two offices, while Let be there and all his at 16.30 are each one unit doing one office, which is how rule 2 divides a supplied run.

One judgment I checked and left: 16.22 marks again added under rule 44's surplus-particle sentence while 16.19 folds off into shaved off, and the same lemma is written bare at 16.17 and 16.22. The two are different lemmas and different particles, so this is not a split, but the subtraction test is closer for off than the note there implies; a later pass revisiting 16.19 should read the note before moving it.

BSB disagreements are all documented convention differences and none is an error. The R, Td, C, To and Sh recurrences are rules 27, 29, 16, 32 and 40 working as written. Of the four singletons: the lamed at 16.2 governs a noun the ASV writes as the bare object of a supplied verb (rule 40); paam at 16.20 is the unrendered half of a repetition the ASV writes once; the suffix at 16.28 is the lexicalized suffix of the divine title (rule 57); the suffix at 16.29 is the resumption the relative carries, as the convention above records.
